description: How a start-up divides its market by age, gender, occupation, income, location and lifestyle.
content_html:
What Is Market Segmentation?

Market segmentation is the process of splitting a broad potential customer base into smaller, more homogeneous groups. Rather than trying to sell to everyone in exactly the same way, a start-up identifies which groups share similar needs and tailors its product, price and promotion to fit those groups specifically. This makes marketing more efficient — the right message reaches the right people, and resources are not wasted on audiences unlikely to buy.

Without segmentation, a start-up risks designing a product that tries to please everyone and ends up satisfying no one, or spending its limited marketing budget reaching people who have no interest in the product. A clear understanding of which customer groups exist and which ones the business is targeting allows the entrepreneur to focus limited resources where they will have the most impact.

The Six Bases of Segmentation

There are six ways a start-up can segment its market: age, gender, occupation, income, location and lifestyle. Each one uses a different characteristic to group customers. A business does not have to use all six — typically, two or three bases are combined to build a clearer picture of the target customer.

Key Fact

The six segmentation bases are: age, gender, occupation, income, location and lifestyle. You need to be able to describe each one and apply it to a specific type of start-up business. Exam questions may ask you to identify which base would be most relevant for a given scenario — always justify your answer with a because-therefore chain.

Age and gender are the most commonly used demographic segmentation variables. Age shapes spending habits, product preferences and the channels through which customers can be reached — a company selling mobility scooters targets older adults, while a social media marketing agency targets younger business owners more comfortable with digital platforms. An entrepreneur selling luxury vinyl records targets a different age group from one selling music streaming gift cards.

Gender — grouping by gender. A barber’s shop in a city centre and a women’s outdoor adventure clothing brand both use gender as a primary segmentation variable. Many businesses have shifted away from rigid gender segmentation as buying patterns have changed, but for some products it remains a highly practical organising variable. A start-up selling beard care products naturally targets male customers; a maternity swimwear brand targets pregnant women.

Occupation — grouping by job type or professional role. A business selling professional chef’s knives targets people who cook for a living; a provider of executive coaching services targets senior managers and directors. Occupation is often combined with income segmentation — professionals in high-skilled roles tend to have higher disposable incomes and may be more willing to spend on quality.

Income — grouping by how much customers earn and what they can afford to spend. Budget supermarkets such as Aldi attract price-sensitive shoppers; premium delicatessens attract higher-income households prepared to pay more for quality and provenance. A start-up must decide which income segment it is targeting before it sets a price — a price too high for its segment will deter buyers; a price too low signals poor quality to premium shoppers.

Location — grouping customers by where they live or work. A local market stall targets customers within a short travel radius. An e-commerce start-up might segment by region to account for differences in delivery cost, dialect in marketing copy, or regional preferences. A Manchester-based vegan bakery would focus its social media advertising on people in Greater Manchester rather than running a national campaign it cannot yet fulfil. Location is often the most practical first segmentation base for a small start-up with limited resources.

Lifestyle segmentation groups customers by what they value and how they live, rather than just by age or income. Two people of the same age and income might live very differently: one prioritises environmental sustainability and buys only ethical products; another prioritises convenience and speed. Lifestyle segmentation allows a start-up to speak directly to the things its target customers care about. A sustainable clothing brand targets customers who prioritise environmental ethics, not simply those in a particular age band or income bracket.

Students sometimes assume that a business should use as many segmentation bases as possible. In practice, over-segmenting can shrink the addressable market so much that there are not enough customers to sustain the business. A start-up targeting only left-handed, vegan, female cyclists aged 25–35 in Winchester has segmented so precisely that the group may be too small. The goal is to find a group large enough to be profitable while specific enough to be reached efficiently. Exam answers that recognise this trade-off score more marks than those that simply describe segmentation as always beneficial.

Why Market Segmentation Benefits a Start-Up

Segmentation delivers six specific benefits that a start-up should understand and be able to apply to a scenario. First, it helps the business meet specific customer needs more accurately — a product designed for a defined group rather than for everyone in general fits that group better and is more likely to convert browsers into buyers.

Second, it can increase profits by allowing the business to charge a price that the target segment is prepared to pay — a premium segment allows premium pricing; a budget segment drives volume. Third, it enables targeted marketing — the start-up spends its limited budget on the channels and messages most likely to reach its defined segment, rather than spreading spend thinly across irrelevant audiences.

Fourth, it improves customer retention — a business whose product genuinely fits its segment’s needs will build a loyal customer base that returns and recommends. Fifth, it can grow market share by establishing a reputation as the go-to brand for that segment, making it harder for competitors to enter the same space. Sixth, it ensures the business is matching its product to specific needs, reducing the risk of stock waste, over-production or mismatch between what is offered and what customers want.

Key Fact

The six benefits of market segmentation for a start-up are: meeting specific customer needs, increasing profits, enabling targeted marketing, improving customer retention, growing market share, and matching the product accurately to what customers want. Exam questions will often ask for two or three of these applied to a specific business scenario.
exam_tip_html: For a 6-mark “analyse” question on segmentation, embed the specific details of the case-study scenario into your answer — the product type, the location, the likely target customer. Naming the business alone does not earn application marks; you need to use the specific characteristics of the business to explain why a particular segmentation base would or would not work. For a 4-mark “explain” question on the benefits of segmentation, use a because–therefore chain: state the benefit, explain the mechanism, then state the outcome for the business. Do not describe segmentation bases in a benefits answer — describe the benefit itself and apply it to the scenario given.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Market segmentation divides a broad market into groups with similar characteristics — the six bases are age, gender, occupation, income, location and lifestyle.
  • The six benefits of segmentation are: meeting specific customer needs, increasing profits, enabling targeted marketing, improving customer retention, growing market share, and matching the product to customer needs.
  • In exam answers, always apply your chosen segmentation base and its benefit to the specific scenario — a description of segmentation without connecting it to the business in the question earns fewer marks.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of lifestyle segmentation?
A) Targeting customers who live within five miles of the shop
B) Targeting customers who earn more than £40,000 per year
C) Targeting customers who prioritise ethical and sustainably made products
D) Targeting female customers aged 18 to 30
practice_questions.marks: C) Targeting customers who prioritise ethical and sustainably made products [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two of the six bases a business can use to segment its market.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark per correct segmentation base, up to 2 marks.

Acceptable answers: age / gender / occupation / income / location / lifestyle.

Do not accept vague answers such as 'by type of customer' unless a specific base is identified.

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by 'occupation' as a basis for market segmentation.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks.
• Occupation segmentation groups customers according to their job type or professional role [1 mark]
• For example, a business selling specialist legal software targets solicitors and barristers rather than the general public [1 mark]

Also accept any example of a business product matching an occupational group.

practice_questions.text: Explain one benefit of market segmentation for a small start-up business. Use the words 'because' or 'therefore' in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks.

Mastering (4 marks): A fully developed because-therefore explanation that identifies a specific benefit, explains the mechanism, and states the outcome for the start-up.

Secure (2-3 marks): The benefit is identified and explained with one development point, but the chain is incomplete.

Developing (1 mark): A benefit is named with no development.

Emerging (0 marks): No relevant content.

Acceptable content (any one benefit fully developed):
• Targeted marketing: because the start-up focuses its advertising on the specific segment most likely to buy, its limited marketing budget is spent more efficiently, therefore reducing wasted spend and increasing the return on every pound invested in promotion.
• Meeting specific customer needs: because the product is designed around a defined group rather than a general market, it fits that group's needs more precisely, therefore customers are more likely to buy and return.
• Increasing profits: because the start-up can pitch its product at a price the target segment is prepared to pay (e.g. a premium segment accepts premium pricing), therefore profit per unit is higher than a one-size-fits-all approach would achieve.

practice_questions.text:
Aiden Cole runs 'Forge & Flint', a small start-up making premium hand-forged kitchen knives in Sheffield. He currently advertises his products to all adults nationwide using social media posts. He is considering switching to a more targeted approach, segmenting his market by occupation (professional chefs and serious home cooks) and income (mid-to-high earners).

Analyse how using these two segmentation bases could improve the performance of Forge & Flint.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks.

Mastering (5–6 marks): A well-developed analytical response that uses specific details from Aiden's scenario (premium knives, Sheffield, social media to all adults, professional chefs and serious home cooks, mid-to-high income) to explain how both segmentation bases would improve marketing efficiency and revenue. A because-therefore chain is present for each base, and at least one limitation is acknowledged.

Secure (3–4 marks): Both bases are analysed with some development. At least one scenario detail used meaningfully. A conclusion or limitation is present.

Developing (1–2 marks): One base described or both mentioned at a surface level.

Emerging (0 marks): No relevant content.

Content guidance:
Occupation (professional chefs): Aiden's premium knives have features that professional chefs value (precision, durability, hand-forged quality). Because this group uses knives for hours every day, they will pay more for a superior tool; therefore focusing on this segment justifies Forge & Flint's premium price.
Income (mid-to-high earners): currently advertising to all adults means reaching many people who cannot afford or would not prioritise a premium knife. Switching to income-based targeting means every advertising pound reaches someone within the price-acceptable range, reducing wasted spend.
Conclusion: combined, the two bases create a much sharper target — a professional cook on a decent income — which should reduce marketing cost per conversion and support the premium positioning.

practice_questions.text:
Mei Zhang is planning to launch 'Verdant Threads', a start-up selling sustainable, naturally dyed children's clothing made from organic cotton. She is deciding whether to segment her market by age (targeting parents of children aged 0-5) or by lifestyle (targeting parents who prioritise environmental sustainability).

Justify which segmentation approach Mei should use for the launch of Verdant Threads.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks.

Mastering (5–6 marks): A well-reasoned recommendation for one approach, using specific details from Mei's scenario (organic cotton, natural dye, sustainability angle, children aged 0-5) to explain why one basis is more appropriate. The conclusion adds evaluative thinking beyond summarising earlier points.

Secure (3–4 marks): A recommendation is made and supported with analysis. At least one scenario detail used. Some acknowledgement of the alternative.

Developing (1–2 marks): A recommendation is present but with limited reasoning.

Emerging (0 marks): No recommendation or relevant analysis.

Content guidance:
Age (parents of 0-5): wider addressable group; easier to identify (new parents are a clearly defined demographic); Facebook groups for parents are accessible and low-cost to target. Drawback: many parents in this group do not prioritise sustainability and would choose cheaper alternatives, so reaching them does not guarantee conversion.
Lifestyle (sustainability-focused parents): smaller but better-matched segment; these parents are actively looking for exactly what Verdant Threads offers; word of mouth within sustainability communities can be powerful; messaging can focus on the ethical story which is Verdant Threads' core differentiator. Drawback: the segment may be smaller, limiting initial volume.
Recommendation: lifestyle segmentation is the stronger choice for launch because the product's key differentiator — organic, sustainably dyed — only appeals to buyers who value that story. Age segmentation alone would waste budget reaching parents who will simply choose cheaper alternatives.

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is an example of occupation-based market segmentation?
options: Targeting customers who live within 10 miles of the business
Targeting customers who earn over £50,000 per year
Targeting professional chefs with a specialist knife brand

knowledge_checks.q: Which of the following is a benefit of market segmentation for a start-up?
options: It guarantees that all customers in the segment will buy the product
It allows the business to reach all possible customers at once
It helps the business focus its limited marketing budget on the most likely buyers
It removes the need to conduct market research

knowledge_checks.q: _____ segmentation groups customers by their values, interests and way of living rather than by age or income alone.
The six bases a business can use to segment its market are age, gender, occupation, income, location and _____.
Match each segmentation base to its correct description:
right: Grouping customers by their job type or professional role
Grouping customers by how much they earn and are willing to spend
Grouping customers by where they live or work

flashcard_questions.a: Dividing a broad market into groups of customers who share similar characteristics.

flashcard_questions.q: Name all six bases a business can use to segment its market.
flashcard_questions.a: Age, gender, occupation, income, location, lifestyle.
Grouping customers by their values, interests and way of living, not just by age or income.
Grouping customers according to their job type or professional role.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does segmentation make a start-up's marketing more efficient?
flashcard_questions.a: Limited budget is spent on audiences most likely to buy, reducing wasted spend.

flashcard_questions.q: How does segmentation help a business increase profits?
flashcard_questions.a: It allows premium pricing for a premium segment or volume pricing for a budget segment.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the benefit of improved customer retention through segmentation?
flashcard_questions.a: A product that genuinely fits a segment's needs builds a loyal, returning customer base.

flashcard_questions.q: Why might over-segmenting damage a start-up?
flashcard_questions.a: The target group becomes so small it cannot generate enough revenue to sustain the business.

flashcard_questions.q: How does income segmentation help a start-up set its price?
flashcard_questions.a: It ensures the price matches what the target group can afford and is willing to spend.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example of location-based segmentation by a small UK start-up.
flashcard_questions.a: A vegan bakery in Manchester targets social media ads only at people in Greater Manchester.

flashcard_questions.q: Cloze: Segmenting a market means a start-up can better match its _____ to the specific _____ of a defined customer group.

glossary_terms.definition: Dividing a market into distinct groups of customers who share similar characteristics and who are likely to respond in similar ways to a product or promotional message.
Grouping customers by their values, interests, activities and how they choose to live their lives, rather than purely by demographic characteristics.
Statistical characteristics of a population used to group customers, including age, gender and occupation.
